chunks: "The voltage goes up because a charged capacitor gets stacked on top of the input, like putting two batteries in series.
In phase one I charge a capacitor from the input, so it holds V in . In phase two I disconnect it from ground and connect its negative plate to V in .
A capacitor's voltage can't change instantly, so its positive plate is now at V in plus V in equals 2 volts in relative to ground.
That plate is connected to the output, so the output sits at 2 volts in and charge flows into the output capacitor. The energy is paid for by current.
Each cycle, the input supplies a packet of charge to charge the flying capacitor and then the same amount again while the capacitor is in series, but only one packet goes to the output.
So input current is twice output current: voltage doubled, current halved, power conserved, minus losses. For bigger multiples you chain stages.
In a diode-capacitor Dickson pump, each stage lifts the node by another clock swing, so N stages give about (N plus 1)V in minus diode drops and droop.
Each added stage adds output resistance, which is why high multiples only work at tiny currents."
